newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euro-MP demands censure of Commission now over BSE.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MP demands censure of Commission now over BSE.

text.p: The European Commission should face an immediate censure motion for its mishandling of the mad cow crisis, a member of a European Parliament inquiry into BSE said on Tuesday.
"Faults were committed. Putting off a decision (on a censure motion) will change nothing," Belgian Socialist Jose Happart told a news conference.

Happart announced he was resigning as the Socialist group coordinator on the committee of inquiry (though not from the committee itself) after the Socialists on Wednesday rejected his advice and voted by a narrow majority to suspend a censure motion until December 1997.

This alternative, proposed by German Green Friedrich-Wilhelm Graefe zu Baringdorf, threatens the Commission with a vote of censure if it fails to comply by December with the committee of inquiry's demands for better consumer protection, food safety and democratic control.
Parliament is due to vote on February 19 on the committee's recommendations, which took five months to draft and look increasingly likely to include some form of censure against the Commission.

Happart condemned as "a nonsense" plans to delay action, either until December or -- as French Socialist Andre Laignel has suggested -- until after Commission President Jacques Santer has told parliament on February 19 how the Commission intends to clean up its act.
"The censure motion is a recognition of past responsibility," he insisted. "Once we've got the proof of responsibility we should have the courage to take action."
"How many deaths must there be before the European Parliament assumes its political responsibilities?" he asked.

He said he would campaign individually for immediate condemnation of the Commission. This would take the form of a censure motion independent of the BSE committee's recommendations and would require the backing of at least 63 Euro-MPs.
The Belgian Socialist said he was confident of finding that support and said he expected his campaign to gather swift momentum once that crucial number was reached.
Happart said that as a responsible Euro-MP, answerable to European Union citizens, he could not support the Socialist group position, which was approved by 25 votes to 22.
The parliament had to give citizens a guarantee that there was an EU institution prepared to defend their interests and safety, he said.

The committee of inquiry believes culpability for the mad cow crisis lies first and foremost with the British government, but it has no powers to censure national administrations. The Commission does have this power.
Happart acknowledged most of the criticisms aimed at the Commission related to events which took place while former Commission president Jacques Delors was at the helm.

But he said the current administration run by president Jacques Santer had contributed to the dangers caused by mad cow disease by failing to sanction the British government, succumbing to pressure from British Prime Minister John Major and refusing to cooperate fully with parliament's committee of inquiry.
The fatal cattle disease BSE (bovine spongiform encephalopathy) was first reported in Britain in 1986.
Since then over 165,000 British cattle have been struck down with the disease, compared with around 300 in the rest of Europe.
Happart predicted human deaths related to BSE could be very high and said Britain and the Commission must in future stop products unfit for human consumption reaching the market.
People buying alcohol or tobacco knew it was bad for their health but they expected meat, potatoes and other foodstuffs to be safe, he said, adding, "When we buy meat, we shouldn't be buying poison".
